about: What a clock offset comes to, read by two test suites:
A browser has to know the station's clock or every fade it draws runs out by
however wrong its own clock is; a station has to know the session leader's or
every fade it *drives* does. Same question, same arithmetic, two
implementations — ws/clock.ts and pult_schema::clock — so this file is what
holds them to each other, as testdata/transforms.json does for the scene graph.
The `samples` half is what both do: stamp the question, halve the round trip,
and keep the sample whose round trip was shortest rather than averaging. A
short round trip is the one least likely to have queued in either direction, so
its midpoint is closest to the truth; a mean is dragged by exactly the samples
worth least. Times are milliseconds on the asking machine's own clock, and
`stationMs` is what the far end said its show clock was.
The `bands` half is the station's alone, and is read only by the Rust suite. A
browser draws a picture and a station drives a rig, so only one of them has to
say what a correction does to a fade that is running while it lands: under 20 ms
apply, over 1000 ms step, in between walk at 5% of real time — and never
backwards at any size, because a backward step falls before a landed fade's t1
and starts a parameter that had arrived moving again.

samples.name: a clock already in step reads as zero
the shortest round trip wins, not the average
a full burst keeps its best, and a slow sixth does not talk it out of it
a station behind the reference gives a negative offset

bands.name: under 20 ms is the estimate's own noise, and applies at once
the middle band is walked at a twentieth of real time
just under a second is still a walk
a second forward is a different clock, and is stepped
backwards is never stepped, however far back it is
a correction from a standing bias walks from where it is
